questions.q: In `template <typename T> T weightedAverage(const T& a, double wa, const T& b, double wb)`, how does the compiler know T should be double when you call weightedAverage(101.25, 0.6, 102.75, 0.4)?
options: It defaults to double unless told otherwise
You must always specify weightedAverage<double>(...) explicitly
Template argument deduction infers T from the types of the arguments passed in
It picks the first type listed in the function signature
questions.explain: The compiler deduces the template argument from the actual argument types at the call site, so an explicit <double> is usually unnecessary.

questions.q: What is N in `template <typename T, std::size_t N> class FixedBuffer`?
options: A second type parameter, like T
A non-type template parameter — a compile-time constant value, not a type
A runtime variable that can change after the object is created
An invalid use of templates; N must always be a type
questions.explain: N is a non-type template parameter: a compile-time value (here, a size) rather than a type, which lets the array size be fixed with zero runtime overhead.

questions.q: Are `FixedBuffer<double, 1024>` and `FixedBuffer<int, 64>` the same compiled type at runtime?
options: Yes, templates are erased to a single generic type at compile time
No — each distinct combination of template arguments generates a completely separate compiled type
Yes, because both have the same number of members
It depends on whether they are used in the same translation unit
questions.explain: Templates are instantiated per unique set of template arguments; each combination produces its own separate type and compiled code, which is why templates have zero runtime dispatch cost but can increase binary size.

questions.q: What problem do C++20 concepts solve for templates?
options: They make templates compile faster at runtime
They let a template be called with any type, including completely invalid ones, without error
They let you state the required constraints on a template parameter up front, producing a clear error immediately when a type doesn't satisfy them
They replace templates entirely with a new language feature
questions.explain: Concepts attach a named, checkable constraint to a template parameter, so misuse is rejected immediately with a readable message instead of a deep, confusing error from inside the template body.

questions.q: In `template <Numeric T> T weightedAverage(T a, double wa, T b, double wb)`, what happens if you call this with `std::string` arguments?
options: It compiles and concatenates the strings
It compiles but produces undefined behavior at runtime
The compiler rejects the call immediately because std::string does not satisfy the Numeric concept
It silently converts the strings to numbers
questions.explain: Numeric constrains T to integral or floating-point types; std::string satisfies neither, so the compiler rejects the call with a constraint-violation error at the call site.
